schools.summary: Augustine reads the verse as prophecy spoken to Christ under the form of a wish: the day of trouble is the hour of 'Father, glorify thy Son,' and the name of the God of Jacob protects him because the younger people belong to him.

Calvin calls the psalm a common prayer of the Church for her king, since the welfare of the whole community centred in David's person; Gill refers the day of trouble to Christ's whole life of sorrows, and above all to the garden and the cross.

Henry notes the propriety of David's writing a form of prayer for the congregation to use on his behalf, and draws from it that the greatest of men may be much in trouble and must be much in prayer; Spurgeon makes the psalm the church's intercession joined to her Lord's.

Clarke lays out the psalm's argument by sections, calls it a dialogue psalm and dates it to the war with the Ammonites and Syrians; Wesley grounds the divine name in the covenant God made with Jacob and his posterity.

Ellicott hears Jacob's own words about the God who answered him in the day of his distress behind the title; Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm between its neighbours, its opening echoing the close of the one before and its intercession pairing with the thanksgiving of the one after.

debates.question: Does the psalm speak of David and his wars, or directly of Christ?

sides.position: of David, as a prayer of the congregation for their king going out to battle
of Christ, the day of trouble being his passion and the psalm the church’s intercession for him

outliers.note: Allegorises the psalm's parts throughout — help from the sanctuary is the making of a sanctified body, the Church, and the burnt offering made fat is the cross turned into the joy of the resurrection.

themes: the name of the God of Jacob

2.pericope_label: Help from the sanctuary and the accepted offering

schools.summary: Gill allows the sanctuary to mean the tabernacle or heaven but inclines to read it as the church of God, matching the Zion of the next clause, and refers the granting of the heart's desire to Christ seeing the travail of his soul.

Clarke reads the sanctuary forward to Christ, in whom God is now to be sought, and distinguishes the minchah as a gratitude-offering from the bloody olah brought as an atonement; Wesley keeps the sanctuary concrete, the tabernacle in Zion toward which Israel directed their prayers.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the verses as liturgy sung while the sacrifice was offered, with a Levite's voice announcing its acceptance and the verb read as a perfect of faith; Ellicott, following scholars who take the memorial word to mean incense, renders it 'accept the incense of all thy minchah.'

debates.question: What does the sanctuary from which help is sent denote?

sides.position: the tabernacle on Zion, where the ark then stood
the church of God, the Zion of the following clause

themes: the meal offering and the burnt offering
grant thee according to thine heart

schools.summary: Gill reads the salvation rejoiced in either as the deliverance Christ himself possesses — chiefly his resurrection, session and intercession — or as the salvation of which he is the author.

Spurgeon presses the resolve: the people rejoiced before their king went out to battle, and much more should we who have seen the victory won; he reads the banner as a standing posture of defiance and the name of Jesus as the church's war-cry.

Clarke puts the words in the mouth of David and his officers consecrating their banners to a just cause, and passes on the etymology deriving Maccabeus from the initials of the song at the sea; Wesley takes the line as an assurance of victory, the banners set up by way of triumph.
Ellicott corrects the verb to 'we will wave our banners' and pictures the army, or its representatives, raising the shout in the Temple courts.

outliers.note: Turns the verse into an argument for habitual joy — 'unbelief begins weeping for the funeral before the man is dead; why should not faith commence piping before the dance of victory begins?'

themes: in the name of our God
the Lord fulfil all thy petitions

schools.summary: Gill denies the anointed is David and takes the whole verse of the Messiah, the church assuring herself that he would be delivered out of all his troubles, raised from the dead and given all power, his members being saved in him.

Henry finds the ground of the assurance in the praying rather than the sacrifice: it is a happy presage when God pours out a spirit of prayer, and the answer takes its rise from heaven, of which the sanctuary was a type, and takes effect below in what God actually performs.

Clarke supposes these the priest's words after the victim was consumed and the signs of acceptance appeared, cautions that David must keep praying if he expects continual salvation, and parses hand, right hand and strength of the right hand by degrees; Wesley reads the tense as certainty grounded in God's power, faithfulness and love.

Ellicott renders it 'now know I that Jehovah hath saved his anointed,' insists the anointed is the king of the poem rather than Israel or an ideal king, and marks the advance from the sanctuary of the opening prayer to God's dwelling-place on high.

debates.question: Who is the anointed whom the Lord saves?

sides.position: the king who is the subject of the psalm; reading Israel or an ideal king here is out of keeping with the rest
the Messiah, anointed king over the holy hill of Zion, not David

themes: the saving strength of his right hand

7.pericope_label: Chariots and horses against the name of the Lord

schools.summary: Gill details what chariots and war-horses could do, including the scythed currus falcati, then turns the verse inward against every external thing men trust for salvation — fleshly privilege, morality, profession and a round of duties.

Spurgeon reads the two ends as a comment on two foundations: God's enemies are uppermost at first but their footing is rotten, while those who rest on Jehovah are cast down at the onset and then uplifted; he takes the psalm's close as a recapitulation of its twofold desire.

Clarke gives the short, emphatic original without the supplied verb, notes that the law allowed David neither chariots nor horses so that his enemies had the advantage, and stages the reversal as a victory already counted on; Wesley glosses remember as trust and has the enemy brought down from what they trusted.

Ellicott says inserting 'trust' weakens the poetry and renders it 'we in the name of Jehovah our God make boast,' seeing a whole battle fought before our eyes; Keil and Delitzsch describe the close as staging, the chorus returning so the song ends as it began.

debates.question: Should the supplied verb "trust" stand in the contrast?

sides.position: no — the original is elliptical and emphatic; render it "we make boast in the name of Jehovah"
the sense of the verb is trust, however the clause is filled out

themes: the name of the Lord our God

schools.summary: Gill rejects the Greek, Ethiopic and Arabic punctuation that draws 'king' up into the opening cry, holding with Aben Ezra that the accent separates the words, and divides the line so that the first petition addresses the Father and the second the King Messiah.

Clarke lays the versions side by side and prefers the Syriac — save David, and David will save us — as the easiest sense; Wesley cuts through the dispute by identifying the king with God himself, the king of kings and in a peculiar manner the king of Israel.

Ellicott holds that the Masoretic accentuation our translators followed spoils the rhythm and interrupts the sense, prefers the Septuagint and Vulgate division giving 'Jehovah, save the king,' and reads the slide into the third person as the Hebrew way of letting a poem die away in subdued language.

debates.question: Where does the pause fall in the closing line, and who is the king?

sides.position: "Jehovah, save the king" — everything refers to God, who hears when we call
the Masoretic accent divides the clauses; the second petition is addressed to the King Messiah
with the Syriac, the king is David, who will hear his people when they call
the king is God himself, the supreme monarch and king of Israel

themes: in the day of our calling
